description: The Global Petrochemical Map is a collaborative public map of petrochemical industrial sites around the world and the communities living and working beside them. It combines emission levels for sites in the US and Europe with a growing set of case reports on specific sites worldwide, covering industrial production, fenceline communities, health and environmental impacts, community mobilisations and industrial disputes, and it invites community members to add their own knowledge. It was built by the Toxic Expertise team at the University of Warwick, whose members David Brown and Lorenzo Feltrin introduced the pilot version, launched in July 2019, and it runs on the Community Maps platform by Mapping for Change. Coverage is global, with sites chosen for geographic spread, economic significance and the intensity of community mobilisation. The map is free online. Caveats: many case reports were compiled by desk research under time limits, the map application returned only a page shell to a non-browser fetch on the access date so its current content could not be checked, and no licence is stated. For simulation it locates petrochemical complexes and their nearby communities for hazard exposure studies of chemical and energy infrastructure. It is related to the Life at the Fenceline record in this catalogue, a US map of people near chemical facilities.
